raw_case_text: A 48-year-old man presented with high-grade fever with chills, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, acholic stools, dark urine, and yellowish discoloration of skin and sclera for one week. His past medical history was significant for diabetes and hypertension. He was immune to hepatitis A and B, with no history of bleeding diathesis nor recent use of new medications. He is a nonsmoker with no history of alcohol consumption. He returned from Pakistan 6 days prior to this admission. On presentation, the patient was ill-appearing, normotensive, and tachycardic (no relative bradycardia) but well perfused with diffuse abdominal tenderness and icteric sclera. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis and elevated creatinine. Liver function tests showed a mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic picture, elevated ammonia levels, and negative hemolytic laboratory parameters (Table 1). Workups for viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and metabolic causes of hepatitis were negative, and serum salicylate levels were within normal range. Ultrasound of the abdomen revealed normal bile duct and gallbladder, and the absence of ascites. Doppler ultrasound ruled out thrombus. The echocardiogram revealed an ejection fraction of 61%-65%. A computerized tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed multiple liver cysts, mesenteric (Figure 1) and porta-hepatis lymphadenopathy (Figure 2), mild thickening of the terminal ileum (Figure 3) and proximal ascending colon. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed severe hepatic steatosis and multiple scattered liver cysts. Empirically ceftriaxone and metronidazole were initiated after obtaining blood cultures. Blood cultures grew Salmonella typhi. Intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone was continued. The patient clinically deteriorated on the above treatment and developed altered mental status, respiratory distress, and showed signs of ALF with an up-trending Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score. He was upgraded to the intensive care unit on Day 3 of admission, requiring on and off high-flow nasal cannula. His blood pressure remained within normal limits. Initially, IV ertapenem was started; however, the patient did not clinically improve and was not clearing the bacteria in the blood cultures, so the antibiotic was switched to IV meropenem on Day 5 of hospitalization due to its frequency of dosing and ability to achieve a comparatively better time to minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC), resulting in clinical recovery (creatinine improved, with hepatorenal syndrome ruled out) and clearance of infection on repeat blood cultures. The first blood cultures drawn grew Salmonella typhi resistant to ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin. It was sensitive to azithromycin. No results were available for carbapenems. The patient completed 2 weeks of IV meropenem in-patient and was discharged after 22 days of hospital stay, stable on discharge, off any antibiotics, with negative blood cultures. One week after discharge, the patient was admitted due to back pain; however, his liver enzymes continued to remain within normal limits.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old male presented with a 1-week history of high-grade fever with chills, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dark urine, acholic stools, and jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed high-grade fevers with chills, diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, acholic stools, dark urine, and yellowish discoloration of the skin and sclera 1 week prior to admission. Six days prior to presentation, he had returned from international travel to Pakistan.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Documented immunity to hepatitis A and B. No history of bleeding diathesis, no new medications, non-smoker, and no alcohol consumption. Travel to Pakistan 6 days prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: High fevers, chills, diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dark urine, pale stools, and jaundice. Denies bleeding tendencies.

objective.physical_examination: Ill-appearing, normotensive, tachycardic without relative bradycardia, and well-perfused. Sclera were icteric. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness. Blood pressure remained within normal limits during admission.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory evaluation demonstrated leukocytosis, elevated serum creatinine, mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury, and elevated serum ammonia levels; hemolytic markers were negative. Serum salicylate levels were within normal range. Serologies for viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis markers, and metabolic causes of hepatitis were all negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal gallbladder and bile ducts without cholelithiasis or ascites. Doppler ultrasound ruled out portal/hepatic vascular thrombosis. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 61%-65%.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT demonstrated multiple hepatic cysts, mesenteric and porta-hepatis lymphadenopathy, and mild mural thickening of the terminal ileum and proximal ascending colon. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) revealed severe hepatic steatosis and multiple scattered liver cysts.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Salmonella typhi bacteremia (typhoid fever) complicated by acute liver failure (ALF) and acute kidney injury, acquired during travel to Pakistan. Blood cultures grew Salmonella typhi with resistance to ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin, and susceptibility to azithromycin (carbapenem breakpoints not available). Viral, autoimmune, and metabolic hepatitis were ruled out; hepatorenal syndrome was ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initially treated empirically with IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole, but clinically deteriorated with altered mental status, worsening ALF (up-trending MELD score), and acute respiratory failure requiring ICU transfer and high-flow nasal cannula support on day 3. Switched to IV ertapenem without clinical or microbiological improvement (persistent bacteremia). Switched on hospital day 5 to IV meropenem to optimize time-above-MIC pharmacodynamics, which led to clinical defervescence, resolution of encephalopathy, normalization of serum creatinine, and clearance of bacteremia on repeat blood cultures. Completed a 2-week inpatient course of IV meropenem and was discharged on hospital day 22 in stable condition off antibiotics. At 1-week follow-up, liver enzymes remained within normal limits.
